nameStory: Chara zeylanica gets its scientific name from the island of Ceylon (now Sri Lanka), where it was first scientifically described. Like other members of the muskgrass family, it can produce a distinctive musky, skunky smell when crushed or disturbed. This earthy odor comes from sulfur compounds the plant produces, making it unmistakable once you've experienced it.
description: Chara zeylanica is an aquatic plant that looks more like a green underwater Christmas tree than a typical plant. It grows completely submerged in freshwater, forming bushy clusters of segmented, branching stems that can reach 12-18 inches tall. Despite being called a stonewort, it's not actually related to true plants with flowers - it's a type of green algae that's evolved to look remarkably plant-like. The whole structure feels rough and gritty to the touch due to calcium carbonate deposits on its surface.

idTips.label: Musky odor
idTips.description: When pulled from water or crushed, produces a strong skunky or garlicky smell that's unmistakable and can be detected from several feet away

idTips.label: Gritty texture
idTips.description: Stems and branches feel rough and sandy between your fingers due to lime deposits, quite different from the smooth feel of most aquatic plants

idTips.label: Whorled branches
idTips.description: Side branches emerge in circular arrangements (whorls) around the main stem, typically 6-8 branches per whorl, creating a layered Christmas tree effect

idTips.label: Segmented stems
idTips.description: Main stems are clearly divided into sections with visible joints, like bamboo but much smaller and more delicate

idTips.label: Brittle when dry
idTips.description: Fresh specimens are flexible underwater but become extremely brittle and crumble easily when dried out

habitat: Found in shallow, clear freshwater lakes, ponds, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, typically in water 1-6 feet deep. Prefers hard water with high mineral content and often grows in areas with sandy or rocky bottoms. Commonly found alongside other submerged aquatics like pondweeds and water milfoils.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins as water warms, with fresh green shoots emerging from overwintered structures. Best time to observe the characteristic branching pattern as plants are actively growing.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with full, bushy growth visible underwater. Reproductive structures may be present as small, round capsules on the branches.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to decline but are still identifiable. The musky odor becomes more pronounced as parts of the plant start to decompose.
seasonality.winter: Most above-ground portions die back, leaving only resting structures in the sediment that are difficult to identify without expertise.

funFact: Chara zeylanica is so good at extracting calcium from water that it essentially builds itself a limestone skeleton while alive, making some specimens heavy enough to sink like rocks when pulled from the water.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other underwater plants like water milfoils or pondweeds, but the distinctive musky smell when disturbed is a dead giveaway - no other aquatic plant produces this skunky odor. Remember: "If it stinks, it's a stonewort."
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called stoneworts and looking like complex plants, these are actually advanced green algae that evolved plant-like structures independently. They're considered living fossils, with relatives dating back over 400 million years, making them much older than flowering plants.
compareHints: Chara zeylanica is extremely rare in New England with only 2 recorded observations, making it much less common than fragile stonewort or common stonewort. It tends to have more robust, thicker stems than delicate stonewort and lacks the distinctive star-shaped reproductive structures of Braun's stonewort. The specific identification often requires microscopic examination of reproductive structures by experts.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Fragile stonewort is distinguished from its relatives like common stonewort and Braun's stonewort primarily through microscopic features of its reproductive structures, which have distinctive surface patterns.
Common stonewort can be distinguished from fragile stonewort by its distinctive spikes between the bark cells - fragile stonewort lacks these tiny projections and feels slightly less rough.
Compared to its relatives, delicate stonewort is the most fragile of the New England stoneworts - much more so than the sturdier common stonewort or even fragile stonewort.

Braun's stonewort differs from its relatives like common stonewort and fragile stonewort by lacking cortication - the bark-like ridged coating that makes other species feel textured along their main stems.
